ground: "The All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving." The two names from the opening formula (1:1) come back right after "Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds" (1:2). In Arabic they are genitive adjectives that still depend on لِلَّهِ, so the praise sentence goes on through them: praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving, and on to the Master of the Day of Judgment (1:4). Both names come from the root of mercy. The first (faʿlān) names mercy that is vast and belongs only to God. The second (faʿīl) names mercy as a lasting quality that reaches the one it is shown to.

findings.statement: God is named the Merciful here in the full sense, and because rabb sits between the womb-rooted names of 1:1 and 1:3, the Lord of the worlds can also be heard held inside a tenderness whose root word is the womb that shelters what grows in it.
findings.perceptible: The Lord is more than an owner over the worlds. He is heard surrounded, before and after, by the language of the womb and of raising. Lordship takes on a bodily, protective and time-bound feel: something carried and grown, not only ruled.

triggers.how: shared root. Maqāyīs gives one root sense (رقة، عطف، رأفة) and says the womb is called raḥim because from it comes the child one feels tender toward. Mufradāt gives the opposite direction: raḥim first, then kinship borrowed from it, 'because they came out of one womb'.

findings.statement: The mercy named here is the plain divine mercy, and the dictionary holds its branches together as one concept: a softness that bends toward, and does good to, what is bound to oneself. The womb, the kin tie and tenderness are three faces of it.
findings.perceptible: Mercy (raḥma) is not pity from above toward a stranger. It is the pull a source feels toward what came from it and stays tied to it. That gives the reader the direction of the mercy: it runs along a bond.

triggers.how: the worlds just named are followed at once by the root of kinship
Mufradāt (entry) quotes the report 'I am al-Raḥmān and you are al-raḥim; I derived your name from My name; whoever joins you I join'. The kin tie is named from this very name.

findings.statement: Al-Raḥmān is the name of God's own vast mercy, and in the dictionary's own report it is also the name from which the kin tie (raḥim) is drawn. So the worlds of 1:2 can be heard as held by one source to which kinship itself goes back.
findings.perceptible: The Turkish reader hears 'Rahman' as a remote title. The Arabic lets them hear that the everyday tie between relatives carries a share of this name. The mercy of 1:3 reaches down into family bonds and gives them their meaning.

triggers.how: syntax: both names are genitive, agreeing with لِلَّهِ; the sentence continues into 1:4 مَٰلِكِ

findings.statement: The two names stand as a verse of their own, yet grammatically they are still inside 'praise belongs to God…'. They describe the One who is praised and, in doing so, give a reason for the praise.
findings.perceptible: 1:2 through 1:4 is one breath: Lord of the worlds, All-Merciful, Mercy-Giving, Master of the Day. Mercy is part of the description of the Praised One, not a separate exclamation. It also sits between universal lordship and the Day of Judgment.

triggers.how: paired with a second form of the same root. The entries compare the pair to nadmān/nadīm. Sihah: two names of different derivation repeated for emphasis, like جادّ مُجِدّ. Jamhara: Arabs say 'kun bī raḥīman' but never 'raḥmānan'.

findings.statement: Both names mean merciful. The first is built for vastness and is used only of God, almost as a proper name. The second is a quality one can ask to be turned toward oneself.
findings.perceptible: The pair moves from breadth to nearness: mercy that covers everything, then mercy that comes close enough to be asked for by a single person. A paraphrase such as 'most merciful' flattens this into one word.

findings.statement: God is merciful without qualification, and because these names come directly before 'Master of the Day of Judgment', the Day where debts are settled is heard as approached through mercy.
findings.perceptible: Order carries meaning: the reader reaches the King of the reckoning only after passing through mercy twice. Judgment is framed by mercy on the side from which it is approached.

triggers.how: Mufradāt (entry): الرحمة من الله إنعام وإفضال, divine mercy is bestowal of favor. B001 definition includes الإحسان إلى المرحوم.
praise returned for favor

findings.statement: The Mercy-Giving is praised for His mercy, and since the dictionary defines His mercy as actually bestowing favor, 1:3 already names the quality that 1:7 will call 'those whom You have favored'.
findings.perceptible: The favor that the surah names only at its end is present here as a quality of the One praised. The praise in 1:2 is answered by 1:3: this is the reason for it, mercy that acts and gives.

triggers.how: Tahdhīb reports Ibn ʿAbbās: both are 'gentle names, one gentler than the other'; al-Raḥīm is العاطف على خلقه بالرزق, the one who bends toward His creatures with provision. This matches rabb's raising and feeding.

findings.statement: The Mercy-Giving is merciful in the full sense, and one old gloss makes that mercy concrete as bending toward creatures with their daily provision, the same care the rabb shows in raising.
findings.perceptible: Mercy becomes visible in what is given to eat and live on, day after day. That ties it to the raising rabb in 1:2 rather than leaving it a feeling.

triggers.how: Tahdhīb (Ibn al-Aʿrābī): God called rain raḥma, because by His mercy it comes down from the sky

findings.statement: The mercy named here is God's mercy in general. The Arabic also knows one concrete form of it, rain sent down, and the Turkish 'rahmet yağıyor' still keeps that sense.
findings.perceptible: For the Turkish reader, their own word for rain ('rahmet') is a way into the ayah. It is not a loss: it shows mercy as something that comes down from above and makes things grow.

triggers.how: concordance collocate وَلَد (child), e.g. 19:88–92, 'they said al-Raḥmān has taken a child', which is denied

findings.statement: The womb-rooted name keeps its tenderness while the Quran, precisely under this name, denies that God begets a child. The womb image describes how the mercy feels, not a birth.
findings.perceptible: This keeps the womb image in its place: it gives mercy its warmth and closeness without suggesting offspring. The same name is used by the Quran to rule that reading out.

findings.perceptible: At most, a sense that mercy toward what one has brought forth is something felt from within. It is too bodily to state of God and is kept only as part of the root's texture.

findings.statement: Al-Raḥīm here is God's name, as in 114 of its 116 uses, and the form can also be shared: the messenger and the believers are called by it. Al-Raḥmān never is.
findings.perceptible: The second name is the one that can be passed on. It is a mercy people can be asked to show one another, while the first stays God's alone.

triggers.how: exact repetition of 1:1:3–4

findings.statement: The same two names that opened in the basmala come back inside the praise, so 'in the name of' at the start and 'praise belongs to' here meet in the same mercy.
findings.perceptible: The repetition is not filler. In 1:1 the names are what one starts under. In 1:3 they are what one praises. The reader passes from beginning in mercy to thanking for mercy.

loaded_words.role: No dominant role; it behaves as a proper name used only of God (entries: لا يدعى به غيره). It is often subject or target (surah 19 especially), and collocates with child, servant, Throne and intercession.
loaded_words.count: 57 uses; 11 in naming formulas like this one
loaded_words.departure: Translations that render it as a mere adjective ('merciful') lose its name-like weight; translations that render it only as a name lose the root's womb and kin sense.

loaded_words.role: A description of God, usually paired with غَفُور or تَوَّاب
loaded_words.count: 114 of 116 describe God; 9:128 the messenger, 48:29 believers
loaded_words.departure: Here it is paired with al-Raḥmān, not with 'forgiving'. The Turkish 'Bağışlayan' borrows the forgiveness role that belongs to ghafūr in other verses.

losses.loses: Its link to the womb (raḥim) and to the kin tie, and the vastness carried by the faʿlān pattern. In Turkish it survives as a name and a man's name.
losses.adds: The feel of a personal name, which hides that it is a description built from a verb root

grammar: Both names are in the genitive, agreeing with لِلَّهِ in 1:2. So 1:2–1:4 is a single sentence: praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving, Master of the Day. Turkish readers hear 1:3 as a standalone exclamation.

The two patterns differ: faʿlān (raḥmān) is vast, used for God alone and almost a proper name; faʿīl (raḥīm) is a lasting quality that can be asked for and shared. Turkish 'Rahman ve Rahîm' hides the difference.
reread: Praise belongs to God, Lord of all the worlds, and the sentence goes on without a break: the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving. The Lord who owns and raises the worlds is described on both sides by a root whose first picture is the womb, the house where the young grows, and the kin tie that comes out of it. So lordship is heard as care that carries and feeds over time. The first name spreads mercy over everything. The second brings it close enough to be asked for, and the dictionary defines this mercy as favor actually given, the favor 1:7 will name. Only after passing twice through this mercy does the sentence reach the Master of the Day of Judgment. The reckoning is approached from the side of mercy, without being any less a reckoning.
